newsitem.title: ETHIOPIA: U.S. says support for Africa crisis force building.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says support for Africa crisis force building.

text.p: Nine countries have agreed in principle to participate in an all-Africa military force to respond to regional crises and the initiative could begin operating in six months, U.S. officials said Wednesday.

The officials, who arrived with U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher from Mali, said five African countries have signalled willingness to provide troops for the force, while four industrial nations would help finance it.

"We estimate that if we get started right away (it would take) four to six months to get the units to the point where they can effectively operate together," a senior U.S. official told reporters with Christopher on a five-nation Africa tour.
He and other officials would not identify the African countries who have signed up to the U.S.-led initiative beyond Mali, whose participation was announced Tuesday in Bamako.

But Christopher in a news conference on arrival in Addis Ababa said he would discuss this issue with Ethiopian Prime Minister Meles Zenawi and as a "leading figure in this region his (Meles) attitude toward it...will be highly significant."
Countries agreeing to help finance the force are Canada, Britain, Ireland and Belgium, as well as the United States, officials said.

Christopher's two-night stop in the Ethiopian capital will focus on conflict resolution efforts in Africa, the U.S.-push for a new U.N. secretary general, Ethiopia's progress toward democracy and Sudan, which Washington accuses of state-sponsored terrorism.
In addition to Meles, he is due to meet Salim Ahmed Salim, the head of the Organisation of African Unity who is mentioned as a possible successor to U.N. chief Boutros Boutros-Ghali.
Christopher will also address the OAU and meet opposition politicians, democratic and human rights activists.
The African Crisis Response Force would be sent to countries where civil war, insurrection or campaigns of genocide threaten mass civilian casualties.
The immediate catalyst is the civil war in Burundi, where U.S. officials say killing and human rights violations remain at an unacceptable level.
The OAU has welcomed the U.S. initiative to train and equipment the force as long as it is not permanent.
But U.S. officials envision the force as a long-term capability, which would not engage in fighting or separate warring factions but could be deployed anywhere crises erupt.

The plan is to gain commitments for up to 10,000 fighters, but officials said they would begin the programme with fewer. "We're looking for quality not quantity. We do not want this to fail," one official said.

Training the force is estimated to cost upwards of $40 million of which Washington would pay 25 percent. More would be needed when the force is deployed. Congress has appropriated $20 million for a U.S. contribution to such an effort.

A U.S. technical team is expected in the next few weeks to visit the African countries who have agreed to join the force to discuss operational details of merging troops of unequal competency and with different equipment and languages.

At his news conference, Christopher said the United States is "pleased to be the partner of the new Ethiopia" and welcomed its "considerable" progress toward democracy and economic reform after a legacy of dictatorship and civil war. But he said much more must be done in the area of press freedoms.
